description_full: Exelon Corporation, a utility services holding company, engages in the energy distribution and transmission businesses in the United States. The company is involved in the purchase and regulated retail sale of electricity and natural gas; transmission and distribution of electricity; and distribution of natural gas to retail customers. It serves residential, commercial, industrial, and public authorities and electric railroads customers. Exelon Corporation was incorporated in 1999 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Exelon Corporation is a large-cap utilities business with a $47.9B market cap on $24.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and -2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $2.3B of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.9%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Value-trap profile (score 59/100): structural revenue/margin decline; leveraged balance sheet under pressure — cheapness may reflect deterioration, not mispricing
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sector_tailwinds: 52 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
